We study score learning from denoising pairs when the data contain a hidden non-Gaussian component. If covariance reveals the component, its subspace can be recovered directly. If covariance is isotropic, the first distinguishing moment has order k^∗, and the learner must extract that moment from clean points and their noisy views. Small-step online SGD on one unit has this exponent up to logarithms.
A two-stage learner uses the curvature of a smoothed denoising loss to recover the hidden direction, then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout. For every even k^∗, it obtains a fixed score gain over the Gaussian baseline from O(d^k^∗/2log d) clean points.
In the covariance-visible regime, the frozen-feature threshold occurs at d^J/J!, while projection onto principal components makes the fitted-model, score-risk and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension. In the covariance-matched experiments, the measured partial-trace overlaps are consistent with the proposed spectral transition. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse shows a d²-like training-set threshold over d=64--192, with fixed validation and calibration overhead.

deepseek.title: The Denoising Mind - The Denoising Mind
deepseek.snippet:
It is almost exactly backwards. No mind — biological or artificial — is ever handed clean and/or complete truth; what arrives is noisy, partial, obscured by the limits of sensing and perception. The deepest science induced lesson of the last decade of AI is that this is not a bug to be overcome. It is the mechanism. A mind builds a world by learning to undo its obfuscation — and then to generate new pieces of that world, verified by persistent embedding, on its own.  

## Three moves: obscure, recover, generate  

The image generators everyone now uses run on a strikingly simple cycle with three moves.  

Obscure (noisification). Take a clean example and add noise, step by step, on a fixed schedule, until it looks like static. This is dilution, not erasure: the noise is well- defined (white Gaussian noise, added by protocol), and at every step the original is still mathematically "in there," only buried. The signal is hidden, not destroyed.  

Recover (denoisification). Train a network to do one humble thing — at any level of fog, guess the direction back toward something clearer — and run it many times, from highly entropic toward structure. To succeed, the network cannot memorize the absolute; it must learn the deep regularities of a whole domain, where plausible things live and where they don't. By only ever practicing recovery, it ends up holding a complete model of the world it was denoising. And the recovery has an order: coarse structure first, fine detail last — gist before grain, components before the composite whole.  

Generate (generativity). Here is the payoff. A system that can recover signal from noise can be handed fresh noise and asked to walk it toward the nearest plausible structure — producing something never seen before but entirely coherent to previous experiences. It does not store pictures; it stores the shape of the possible, and samples new, plausible variants from it. This is the best we can, and do do, given our resources constraints.

# Denoising Is Stein: Moment Access and a Resource Hierarchy for Learning Hidden Structure in Diffusion Models

We study score learning from denoising pairs when the data contain a hidden non-Gaussian component. If covariance reveals the component, its subspace can be recovered directly. If covariance is isotropic, the first distinguishing moment has order
k∗, and the learner must extract that moment from clean points and their noisy views. Correlations in the denoising loss are Stein discrepancies against a baseline; for polynomial fields they determine exactly the corresponding moment differences. Averaging fresh noisy views conditional on a clean point gives an exact moment query on the clean distribution. In the covariance-matched regime, orientation-independent dictionaries satisfying an L4/L2 condition need order dk∗−1 features, and the stated dot-product kernel ridge models need the same power in samples. Small-step online SGD on one unit has this exponent up to logarithms. A two-stage learner uses the curvature of a smoothed denoising loss to recover the hidden direction, then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout. For every even k∗, it obtains a fixed score gain over the Gaussian baseline from O(dk∗/2logd) clean points. In the covariance-visible regime, the frozen-feature threshold occurs at dJ/J!, while projection onto principal components makes the fitted-model, score-risk and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension. In the covariance-matched experiments, the measured partial-trace overlaps are consistent with the proposed spectral transition. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse shows a d2-like training-set threshold over d=64--192, with fixed validation and calibration overhead.

Contributions of this work:Our key findings can be highlighted as follows:

* ***Inductive bias towards Gaussian structures (Section 3).** Diffusion models in the _generalization regime_ exhibit an inductive bias towards learning diffusion denoisers that are close (but not equal) to the optimal denoisers for a multivariate Gaussian distribution, defined by the empirical mean and covariance of the training data. This implies the diffusion models have the inductive bias towards capturing the Gaussian structure (covariance information) of the training data for image generation.

* ***Model Capacity and Training Duration (Section 4)** We show that this inductive bias is most pronounced when the model capacity is relatively small compared to the size of the training data. However, even if the model is highly overparameterized, such inductive bias still emerges during early training phases, before the model memorizes its training data. This implies that early stopping can prompt generalization in overparameterized diffusion models.

* ***Connection between Strong Generalization and Gaussian Structure (Section 5).** Lastly, we argue that the recently observed strong generalization [20] results from diffusion models learning certain common low-dimensional structural features shared across non-overlapping datasets. We show that such low-dimensional features can be partially explained through the Gaussian structure.

jina.snippet:
Diffusion models learn by seeing a clean example next to a corrupted view of it, and from those pairs they must infer enough hidden structure to estimate the score, the gradient of the log density. The difficulty is that structure can be hidden in two different ways. In one dataset, a special direction shows up in the covariance. In another, the covariance is exactly isotropic, just like a Gaussian's, even though the distribution still differs along that direction. The paper's central move is to extract information from denoising correlations and to revisit each clean point under fresh noise. With that, an explicit two-stage learner finds the hidden direction in the harder regime at a clean-sample cost far below what earlier analyses of other learners suggested.

In panel (a), clean points lie along a line labeled $u$, with arrows linking selected clean points to noisy views; the line is visible in covariance. Panel (b) shows the covariance-matched cloud, where blue and orange mark mixture components for illustration only, since the learner does not observe labels. Panel (c) plots density against projection onto the hidden direction: the clean mixture differs from its mean-and-variance-matched Gaussian, and diffusion at $t = 0.3$ weakens but does not erase the difference. This is a schematic, not a learning result.

A denoiser estimates the score through Tweedie's formula. The denoising loss correlates a residual with a test field, which acts like a Stein discrepancy: it measures how the noisy data law differs from a chosen baseline. For polynomial test fields, these correlations determine the corresponding moment differences. Using a moment-matched Gaussian as the baseline removes every moment the data share with a Gaussian. jina.title: Deconstructing Denoising Diffusion Models for Self-Supervised Learning
jina.snippet:
## Abstract

In this study, we examine the representation learning abilities of Denoising Diffusion Models (DDM) that were originally purposed for image generation. Our philosophy is to deconstruct a DDM, gradually transforming it into a classical Denoising Autoencoder (DAE). This deconstructive process allows us to explore how various components of modern DDMs influence self-supervised representation learning. We observe that only a very few modern components are critical for learning good representations, while many others are nonessential. Our study ultimately arrives at an approach that is highly simplified and to a large extent resembles a classical DAE. We hope our study will rekindle interest in a family of classical methods within the realm of modern self-supervised learning.

# Structured Denoising Diffusion Models in Discrete State-Spaces Jacob Austin ⇤

, Daniel D. Johnson ⇤

, Jonathan Ho, Daniel Tarlow & Rianne van den Berg †

Google Research, Brain Team 

{jaaustin,ddjohnson,jonathanho,dtarlow,riannevdberg}@google.com 

## Abstract 

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) [17] have shown impressive results on image and waveform generation in continuous state spaces. Here, we introduce Discrete Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (D3PMs), diffusion-like generative models for discrete data that generalize the multinomial diffusion model of Hoogeboom et al. [18], by going beyond corruption processes with uni-form transition probabilities. This includes corruption with transition matrices that mimic Gaussian kernels in continuous space, matrices based on nearest neighbors in embedding space, and matrices that introduce absorbing states. The third al-lows us to draw a connection between diffusion models and autoregressive and mask-based generative models. We show that the choice of transition matrix is an important design decision that leads to improved results in image and text domains. We also introduce a new loss function that combines the variational lower bound with an auxiliary cross entropy loss. For text, this model class achieves strong results on character-level text generation while scaling to large vocabularies on LM1B. On the image dataset CIFAR-10, our models approach the sample quality and exceed the log-likelihood of the continuous-space DDPM model.

Training provides __denoising pairs__ $(X_{0},X_{t})$: a clean point and a noisy view. The learner predicts $X_{0}$ from $X_{t}$, thereby estimating the score (Vincent, 2011). If the data have a hidden non-Gaussian direction, a successful denoiser must detect it through those pairs. The amount of data needed depends on what the learner can represent and whether it can use repeated views of the same clean point.

> __Which moments of a hidden structure can a denoising learner access, and how do representation size, distinct clean samples, noisy views and the learner’s access to geometry determine the cost of improving on the Gaussian score?__
We study two versions of one hidden-component model. Data are $X_{0}=UZ+\sigma_{0}(I-UU^{\top})G_{0}$ with an unknown orthonormal $U\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$, a non-Gaussian latent vector $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ and an independent Gaussian $G_{0}$. In the __covariance-visible__ regime ($\sigma_{0}=0$), the data lie on the subspace, their covariance reveals $U$, and principal components recover it from $k+1$ points. In the __covariance-matched__ regime, $\mathrm{Cov}(Z)=\sigma_{0}^{2}I_{k}$, so $\mathrm{Cov}(X_{0})=\sigma_{0}^{2}I_{d}$ carries no information about $U$. The first informative moment has order $k^{\ast}\geq 3$, the __generative exponent__ of the latent law.

# Denoising Is Stein: Moment Access and a Resource Hierarchy for Learning Hidden Structure in Diffusion Models
## Abstract
We study score learning from denoising pairs when the data contain a hidden non-Gaussian component. If covariance reveals the component, its subspace can be recovered directly. If covariance is isotropic, the first distinguishing moment has order k^∗, and the learner must extract that moment from clean points and their noisy views. Correlations in the denoising loss are Stein discrepancies against a baseline; for polynomial fields they determine exactly the corresponding moment differences. Averaging fresh noisy views conditional on a clean point gives an exact moment query on the clean distribution. In the covariance-matched regime, orientation-independent dictionaries satisfying an L^4/L^2 condition need order d^(k^∗−1) features, and the stated dot-product kernel ridge models need the same power in samples. Small-step online SGD on one unit has this exponent up to logarithms. A two-stage learner uses the curvature of a smoothed denoising loss to recover the hidden direction, then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout. For every even k^∗, it obtains a fixed score gain over the Gaussian baseline from O(d^(k^∗/2)log d) clean points. In the covariance-visible regime, the frozen-feature threshold occurs at d^J/J!, while projection onto principal components makes the fitted-model, score-risk and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension. In the covariance-matched experiments, the measured partial-trace overlaps are consistent with the proposed spectral transition. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse shows a d^2-like training-set threshold over d=64–192, with fixed validation and calibration overhead.

# SharedSAE: a unified sparse dictionary across u-net blocks and denoising time for diffusion models

arXiv:2610.13997
Authors: Longhao Lei, Lan Yao
Submitted: 2026-09-27
Subjects: cs.CV cs.AI cs.LG

Abstract

Concept representations in diffusion models drift across network depth and denoising time, yet existing sparse autoencoders offer only per-block or per-timestep dictionaries, leaving no single feature dictionary for localization and intervention in the network. We present Shared Sparse Autoencoder (SharedSAE), which learns one sparse dictionary shared across four U-Net attention blocks and all 50 denoising steps of SDXL 1.0. A block-specific low-rank input adapter aligns the residual distribution of each block before the shared encoder, and a temporal conditioning module with a shared timestep branch and a block-timestep correction branch absorbs temporal non-stationarity. Despite spanning both axes, Shared SAE preserves a coherent dictionary structure. Built on the shared dictionary, localized feature suppression reduces the number of NudeNet-positive generations in the I2P detector-positive subset from 139 to 1. Tracing sparse features across the trajectory further reveals that concept representations are redistributed across U-Net blocks during generation, shifting from the earliest downsampling block toward intermediate and later blocks as denoising proceeds. SharedSAE thus provides a unified, interpretable, and intervention-ready representation space for diffusion models, enabling concept analysis and erasure at any covered block and denoising step.

View PDF HTML (experimental)Abstract:High-dimensional data must be highly structured to be learnable. Although the compositional and hierarchical nature of data is often put forward to explain learnability, quantitative measurements establishing these properties are scarce. Likewise, accessing the latent variables underlying such a data structure remains a challenge. In this work, we show that forward-backward experiments in diffusion-based models, where data is noised and then denoised to generate new samples, are a promising tool to probe the latent structure of data. We predict in simple hierarchical models that, in this process, changes in data occur by correlated chunks, with a length scale that diverges at a noise level where a phase transition is known to take place. Remarkably, we confirm this prediction in both text and image datasets using state-of-the-art diffusion models. Our results show how latent variable changes manifest in the data and establish how to measure these effects in real data using diffusion models.

Abstract: Can a pretrained denoising model replace the dataset used to train it? Hidden Structure in Diffusion Models
Rui Wang
wangrui@microsoft.com
Vancouver, BC, Canada
Abstract
We study score learning from denoising pairs with a hidden non-Gaussian component.
In one regime covariance reveals it; in another, isotropic covariance hides it until the first distinguishing moment, of order k∗.
Denoising-loss correlations are Stein discrepancies against a baseline and, for polynomial fields, exactly encode moment differences.
Averaging noisy views of each clean point gives exact moment queries.
In the covariance-matched regime, orientation-independent dictionaries satisfying an
L4/L2 condition need order dk∗−1 features.
The stated dot-product kernel ridge models need the same power in samples, as does small-step online SGD on one unit up to logarithms.
A two-stage learner uses Gaussian-smoothed-loss curvature to recover the direction, then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout.
For even k∗, it obtains a fixed score gain over the
Gaussian baseline from O(dk∗/2 log d) clean points.
In the covariance-visible regime, the frozen-feature threshold is dJ/J!; projection onto principal components makes fitted-model, score-risk, and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension.
Experiments are consistent with the spectral transition.
A width-8 network trained
with clean-point reuse shows a d2-like training-set threshold over d = 64–192, with fixed
validation and calibration overhead.

The amount of data needed depends on what the learner can represent and whether it can use repeated views of the same clean point.
...
Which moments of a hidden structure can a denoising learner access, and how do representation size, distinct clean samples, noisy views and the learner’s access to geometry determine the cost of improving on the Gaussian score?

seltz.snippet:
The fundamental insight of diffusion models is this: if you have a process that gradually destroys structure, you can learn its reverse to build structure back.

Consider what happens when you gradually add Gaussian noise to an image. At first, the image is recognizable but slightly grainy. After more noise is added, the details blur and only global structure remains. Continue adding noise, and eventually you have something indistinguishable from pure random static, regardless of what the original image was. This forward process destroys information in a principled, mathematically tractable way.

Now flip the perspective. If you could learn to undo each small noise step, you could start with pure random noise and gradually recover a coherent image. You do not need to generate a complete image in one shot; you only need to denoise slightly at each step. This is dramatically more tractable because each denoising step is a small, local change to a partially formed image, rather than a jump from noise to image.

Image generation used to be easy to describe and hard to train. A generator would take a random vector and try to turn it into a realistic image. If the image looked wrong, the training signal had to explain what was wrong. That sounds reasonable until you remember how many ways an image can fail. The subject can be distorted, the texture can be weak, the pose can collapse, the background can look fake, or the image can be sharp but repetitive. A single image is not one decision. It is a large collection of decisions that need to agree.

Diffusion models became important because they change the shape of the problem. Instead of asking a neural network to create a full image in one shot, they ask it to solve a much smaller task many times: given a noisy image, predict how to remove a little of the noise. The same model repeats that correction from heavy noise to a clean image. This makes generation feel less like a leap and more like a guided recovery process.

This chapter starts with the older ideas because they explain why diffusion was such a useful turn. GANs showed that learned generators could make sharp, impressive images, but adversarial training could be fragile. VAEs showed that a model could learn a useful latent space, but samples often looked too smooth. Diffusion combines a different training target with a gradual sampling process. It is not free, since sampling can require many network calls, but the training signal is simple, stable, and visually powerful.

## Introduction

Modern diffusion models increasingly use Transformers, whose attention cost grows quadratically with the number of input tokens. Latent diffusion reduces this cost by compressing an image into a smaller spatial grid and applying diffusion there (34). Our goal is to make extreme spatial compression competitive for latent diffusion. Stronger spatial compression produces fewer tokens. Channel count is a separate design choice, but preserving reconstruction quality typically requires adding channels as the grid shrinks, producing increasingly *wide* latents. This trade is attractive because shorter sequences can substantially reduce denoiser cost, permitting more optimization and sampling under a fixed compute budget. This suggests an obvious strategy: compress the spatial grid as aggressively as possible, then add enough channels to preserve reconstruction quality.

Unfortunately, this strategy encounters a well-established reconstruction-generation dilemma (39; 5; 6; 19). At fixed spatial compression, adding channels improves reconstruction but makes the resulting latent harder to generate. Additional channels let the encoder preserve more image-specific information, including exact textures and local details. This lowers reconstruction error, but increases the information that the diffusion model must produce (6; 11). Standard latent diffusion therefore faces a poor choice: use fewer channels and sacrifice reconstruction quality, or preserve more detail and sacrifice generation quality. Existing approaches reduce this tension by restricting latent information or importing pretrained semantic structure (15; 40; 39; 42; 29). *Ask a language model for a sentence whose syntactic parse is exactly (S (NP * *) (VP * (NP * *))). Before this paper, the strongest plug-and-play method matched the target parse with an F1 of 17.9 out of 100.*

Fine-tuning is the obvious way to control generation: collect pairs of (requirement, text), train the model on them, and it learns to obey. That works. It is also expensive, and it leaves you with one model per requirement, so if you ask for text that is both about Japanese food *and* shaped like a particular sentence, your only option is to multiply the two fine-tuned models together, which the paper shows composes badly.

The alternative keeps the language model frozen and steers it at decoding time with a separate scorer, which is called **plug-and-play** control: the language model supplies fluency, an external classifier supplies the requirement, and you sample from the product. Nothing is retrained, and two classifiers compose by adding their scores. For coarse attributes like sentiment or topic this works; for anything positional it has not.

Diffusion-LM changes what is being steered. Instead of a sequence of discrete token choices, generation becomes a trajectory of continuous vectors, refined from Gaussian noise down to word embeddings over two thousand steps. Continuous means differentiable, so a classifier can be attached to those vectors and its gradient can move them directly.

An image generator begins every picture as television static. Pure random noise, no mountain, no face, no hint of a subject. Twenty or thirty small steps later there is a photograph-quality landscape, and the only thing that changed between those two states is that a neural network repeatedly guessed which parts of the picture were noise and took a little of it away.

That sounds like it should not work, and the history of the idea is a story of researchers noticing that it does. This post builds the intuition first, then the precise mechanism: how the network is trained, how your text prompt steers it, why modern models work in a compressed space, and what changed with the newer transformer-based generators. It is part of The Model Shelf series, and it leans on attention and embeddings, both covered earlier.

## The intuition: learn to undo damage

Take a photograph and add a pinch of random noise. You can still see the picture. Add more and it grows grainy. Keep going for a thousand rounds and nothing of the photo remains; you hold a field of random values with a particular statistical shape, a Gaussian.

Running that process forwards is trivial, since adding noise needs no intelligence. The interesting direction is backwards. If a network could look at a noisy image and say what the slightly less noisy version looks like, you could start from pure noise and walk the chain home. At no point does the network need to produce a whole picture from nothing. Each step only asks for a modest correction, which is an easier problem than drawing.

seltz.title: Diffusion model
seltz.snippet:
In machine learning, **diffusion models**, also known as **diffusion-based generative models** or **score-based generative models**, are a class of latent variable generative models. A diffusion model consists of two major components: the forward diffusion process, and the reverse sampling process. The goal of diffusion models is to learn a diffusion process for a given dataset, such that the process can generate new elements that are distributed similarly as the original dataset. A diffusion model models data as generated by a diffusion process, whereby a new datum performs a random walk with drift through the space of all possible data. A trained diffusion model can be sampled in many ways, with different efficiency and quality.

There are various equivalent formalisms, including Markov chains, denoising diffusion probabilistic models, noise conditioned score networks, and stochastic differential equations. They are typically trained using variational inference. The model responsible for denoising is typically called its "backbone". The backbone may be of any kind, but they are typically U-nets or transformers.

As of 2024, diffusion models are mainly used for computer vision tasks, including image denoising, inpainting, super-resolution, image generation, and video generation. These typically involve training a neural network to sequentially denoise images corrupted by Gaussian noise. The model is trained to reverse the process of adding noise to an image. After training to convergence, it can be used for image generation by starting with an image composed of random noise, and applying the network iteratively to denoise the image.

Diffusion-based image generators have seen widespread commercial interest, such as Stable Diffusion and DALL-E. These models typically combine diffusion models with other models, such as text-encoders and cross-attention modules to allow text-conditioned generation.

# Denoising Is Stein: Moment Access and a Resource Hierarchy for Learning Hidden Structure in Diffusion Models
## Abstract
We study score learning from denoising pairs when the data contain a hidden non-Gaussian component. If covariance reveals the component, its subspace can be recovered directly. If covariance is isotropic, the first distinguishing moment has order k^∗, and the learner must extract that moment from clean points and their noisy views. Correlations in the denoising loss are Stein discrepancies against a baseline; for polynomial fields they determine exactly the corresponding moment differences. Averaging fresh noisy views conditional on a clean point gives an exact moment query on the clean distribution. In the covariance-matched regime, orientation-independent dictionaries satisfying an L^4/L^2 condition need order d^(k^∗−1) features, and the stated dot-product kernel ridge models need the same power in samples. Small-step online SGD on one unit has this exponent up to logarithms. A two-stage learner uses the curvature of a smoothed denoising loss to recover the hidden direction, then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout. For every even k^∗, it obtains a fixed score gain over the Gaussian baseline from O(d^(k^∗/2)log d) clean points. In the covariance-visible regime, the frozen-feature threshold occurs at d^J/J!, while projection onto principal components makes the fitted-model, score-risk and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension. In the covariance-matched experiments, the measured partial-trace overlaps are consistent with the proposed spectral transition. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse shows a d^2-like training-set threshold over d=64–192, with fixed validation and calibration overhead.
